items.prose: A quote on an electronic venue lives for $T$ seconds before it is hit or cancelled. A model gives $T$ the density $f(t) = c(3 - t)$ on $[0, 3]$, and 0 elsewhere.

parts.question: What value of $c$ makes $f$ a density? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set the total area under $f$ equal to 1.

byKey.height: You made the height at $t = 0$ equal to 1. A density needs area 1, not height 1.
byKey.no-half: You took the area as base times height. A triangle has half that.
byKey.reciprocal: That is the area for $c = 1$. Divide 1 by it to find $c$.

explain.text: A density must have total area 1. Here the area is a triangle of base 3 and height $3c$, so $4.5c = 1$. That gives $c = \tfrac{2}{9} \approx 0.2222$, a height of $\tfrac{2}{3}$ at $t = 0$.

parts.question: Using $f(t) = \tfrac{2}{9}(3 - t)$ from part 1, what is $P(T > 2)$, the chance a quote lives more than 2 seconds? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the area under $f$ from 2 to 3.

byKey.left: That is $P(T \le 2)$, the area from 0 to 2. The question asks for the tail.
byKey.height: That is $f(2)$, the height of the density at 2. A chance is an area.
byKey.width: That is the share of the width, as for a uniform. This density falls to 0 at 3, so the tail is thin.

explain.text: The tail from 2 to 3 is a small triangle of base 1 and height $f(2) = \tfrac{2}{9}$. Its area is $\tfrac12 \times 1 \times \tfrac29 = \tfrac19 \approx 0.1111$. In general $P(T > t) = \tfrac{(3 - t)^2}{9}$ on $[0, 3]$.

parts.question: Using the same density, what is $E[T]$, the mean life of a quote in seconds? Give the exact value.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Integrate $t\,f(t)$ over $[0, 3]$.

byKey.midpoint: That is the midpoint of $[0, 3]$, the mean of a uniform. This density leans towards short lives.
byKey.no-c: You integrated $t(3 - t)$ and left out $c = \tfrac{2}{9}$.

explain.text: $E[T] = \tfrac{2}{9}\int_0^3 (3t - t^2)\,dt = \tfrac{2}{9}\left[\tfrac{3t^2}{2} - \tfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^3$. That is $\tfrac{2}{9}(13.5 - 9) = 1$ second. The mean sits left of the midpoint 1.5 because short lives are likelier.

parts.question: A colleague prefers an exponential life with the same mean, so $\lambda = 1$ from part 3. Under his model, what is $P(T > 2)$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. An exponential with rate $\lambda$ has $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$.

byKey.triangle: That is the triangle's answer from part 2. Under the exponential the tail is $e^{-\lambda t}$.
byKey.cdf: That is $P(T \le 2) = 1 - e^{-2}$. Take the tail.
byKey.from-midpoint: That uses a mean of 1.5, so $\lambda = \tfrac{2}{3}$. Part 3 gave a mean of 1.

explain.text: An exponential with mean 1 has $\lambda = 1$ and tail $P(T > t) = e^{-t}$. So $P(T > 2) = e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$. The exponential has no upper limit, so it keeps more chance in the long tail than the triangle.

parts.question: A quote has lived 2 seconds. Back on the triangle, using $P(T > t) = \tfrac{(3 - t)^2}{9}$ and part 2's $\tfrac19$, what is $P(T > 2.5 \mid T > 2)$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: The exponential would give $e^{-0.5} \approx 0.6065$. The triangle gives $\dfrac{0.25/9}{1/9} = 0.25$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide $P(T > 2.5)$ by $P(T > 2)$.

byKey.memoryless: That is the exponential's $e^{-0.5}$, which forgets the 2 seconds. The triangle does not.
byKey.unconditional: That is $P(T > 2.5)$ from the start. We know the quote lived 2 seconds, so divide by $\tfrac19$.
byKey.fresh: That is $P(T > 0.5)$, the chance a new quote lasts half a second. This quote is already 2 seconds old.

explain.text: $P(T > 2.5) = \tfrac{0.5^2}{9} = \tfrac{0.25}{9}$, and dividing by $P(T > 2) = \tfrac19$ gives 0.25. A fresh quote lasts another half second with chance $\tfrac{2.5^2}{9} \approx 0.6944$, so age matters here. The triangle is not memoryless: every quote is gone by 3 seconds.

items.prose: A share trades at £80. Its price in a year is $S_1 = 80\,e^{(m - \sigma^2/2) + \sigma Z}$ with $Z \sim N(0, 1)$, drift $m = 6\%$ and volatility $\sigma = 30\%$ a year.

parts.question: What is the median of $S_1$, in pounds? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The log drift is $0.06 - \tfrac{0.3^2}{2} = 0.015$, so the median is $80e^{0.015} \approx 81.21$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The median of $S_1$ is where $Z = 0$.

byKey.mean: That is the mean, $80e^{0.06}$. The median keeps the drag: $80e^{0.015}$.
byKey.today: That is today's price. The log drift $0.06 - 0.045 = 0.015$ is positive, so the median is a little higher.
byKey.plus-drag: You added $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$ instead of taking it away. The log drift is $m - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2} = 0.015$.

explain.text: Half of $Z$ lies below 0, so half of $S_1$ lies below $80e^{0.015}$. The median passes straight through the exponential: $80e^{0.015} \approx \text{£}81.21$. The $-\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2} = -0.045$ is the volatility drag.

parts.question: Part 1's median was £81.21. What is $E[S_1]$, in pounds? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A lognormal's mean is $e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$.

byKey.median: That is the median from part 1. The mean adds back $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$.
byKey.full-variance: You added the whole $\sigma^2 = 0.09$ to the median's exponent. The mean adds $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$.

explain.text: The mean of a lognormal is $e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$, and here $\mu = \ln 80 + 0.015$. Adding $\tfrac{0.09}{2}$ undoes the drag, so $E[S_1] = 80e^{0.06} \approx \text{£}84.95$. The mean sits above the median, carried by the long right tail.

parts.question: Using £84.95 from part 2, what is $P(S_1 < 84.95)$, the chance the share ends the year below its expected price? Use $\Phi(0.15) = 0.5596$. Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take logs, then standardise with the log drift 0.015.

byKey.half: That treats the mean as the median. The mean is above the median, so more than half the years end below it.
byKey.above: That is $P(S_1 > 84.95)$. The question asks for the chance of ending below.

explain.text: Take logs: $\ln(S_1/80) \sim N(0.015, 0.3^2)$, and $\ln(84.95/80) = 0.06$. So $z = \tfrac{0.06 - 0.015}{0.3} = 0.15$ and $P(S_1 < 84.95) = \Phi(0.15) = 0.5596$. More years than not end below the expected price.

parts.question: A digital option pays if $S_1 > 100$. Using the log drift 0.015 from part 1, find $z$ for a price of £100 to the nearest 0.01. With $\Phi(0.69) = 0.7549$, what is $P(S_1 > 100)$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Standardise $\ln(100/80)$ with the log drift and the volatility.

byKey.phi: That is $\Phi(0.69) = P(S_1 < 100)$. The option pays above £100, so take it from 1.
byKey.no-drag: You standardised with the drift 0.06, which gives $z \approx 0.54$. The log drift is 0.015.
byKey.plus-drag: You used $0.06 + 0.045$ as the log drift. Take the drag away: $0.06 - 0.045 = 0.015$.

explain.text: $\ln(100/80) = \ln 1.25 \approx 0.2231$, so $z = \tfrac{0.2231 - 0.015}{0.3} \approx 0.69$. The option pays with chance $1 - \Phi(0.69) = 0.2451$, about one year in four. The unrounded $z = 0.6938$ gives 0.2439.

parts.question: The desk wants the 95% value at risk of one share over the year: today's £80 minus the price the share stays above with chance 0.95. Using the log drift 0.015 and $P(Z < -1.645) = 0.05$, what is that VaR in pounds? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The 5% price is $80e^{-0.4785} \approx 49.58$, so the VaR is $80 - 49.58 = 30.42$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the price at $z = -1.645$, then take it from £80.

byKey.no-drag: You used the drift 0.06 in the exponent. The log drift is 0.015.
byKey.two-tailed: You used 1.96, which leaves 2.5% in each tail. The VaR needs 5% in the lower tail: 1.645.
byKey.from-mean: You measured the loss from the mean £84.95. The VaR here is measured from today's £80.
byKey.normal-price: That is $1.645 \times 0.3 \times 80$, a normal model of the price. Here the log price is normal.

explain.text: Prices and $z$ move together, so the 5% price is $80e^{0.015 - 1.645 \times 0.3} \approx \text{£}49.58$. The share falls more than £30.42 in a year with chance 0.05. A normal model of the price itself would give £39.48 and ignore that a price cannot go below 0.

items.prose: A desk models its daily P&L $X$, in £k, with the density $f(x) = \tfrac{6 - |x|}{36}$ on $[-6, 6]$, and 0 elsewhere.

parts.question: What is $P(X < -3)$, the chance of losing more than £3k in a day? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: The tail is a triangle of base 3 and height $\tfrac{3}{36}$, so $P(X < -3) = \tfrac12 \times 3 \times \tfrac{3}{36} = 0.125$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the area under $f$ to the left of $-3$.

byKey.no-half: You took base times height. The tail is a triangle, so halve it.
byKey.height: That is $f(-3) = \tfrac{3}{36}$, a height. A chance is an area.
byKey.complement: That is $P(X \ge -3)$. The question asks for the left tail.

explain.text: Below $-3$ the density falls in a straight line from $\tfrac{3}{36}$ to 0 at $-6$. That triangle has area $\tfrac12 \times 3 \times \tfrac{1}{12} = 0.125$. In general $P(X < -v) = \tfrac{(6 - v)^2}{72}$ for $0 \le v \le 6$.

parts.question: The density is symmetric, so $E[X] = 0$. Part 1 found the left tail; now the spread. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$? Give the exact value.

feedback.generic: Not quite. With mean 0, the variance is $E[X^2]$.

byKey.one-side: You integrated over $[0, 6]$ only. The left half adds the same again.
byKey.sd: That is the standard deviation $\sqrt{6}$. The question asks for the variance.
byKey.uniform: That is $\tfrac{12^2}{12}$, the variance of a uniform on $[-6, 6]$. This density is thinner at the ends.

explain.text: With mean 0, the variance is $E[X^2]$. By symmetry it is twice the integral over $[0, 6]$: $\tfrac{2}{36}\left[2x^3 - \tfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^6 = \tfrac{2}{36}(432 - 324) = 6$. So the sd is $\sqrt6 \approx 2.4495$, in £k.

parts.question: Using the left tail $P(X < -v) = \tfrac{(6 - v)^2}{72}$ from part 1, what is the desk's 95% VaR: the loss $v$ with $P(X < -v) = 0.05$? Give £k to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set the tail equal to 0.05 and solve for $v$.

byKey.half-area: You solved $\tfrac{(6 - v)^2}{36} = 0.05$. The tail has 72 underneath, from the half in the triangle's area.
byKey.ten-pc: That leaves 0.1 in the left tail. The 95% VaR leaves 0.05.

explain.text: Set $\tfrac{(6 - v)^2}{72} = 0.05$, so $(6 - v)^2 = 3.6$. Then $v = 6 - \sqrt{3.6} \approx 4.10$. The desk loses more than £4.10k on 1 day in 20.

parts.question: A colleague swaps the density for a normal with the same mean and variance, $N(0, 6)$ from part 2. Using $P(Z < -1.645) = 0.05$, what is his 95% VaR in £k? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The 5% point is 1.645 sds below the mean.

byKey.variance: You multiplied 1.645 by the variance 6. Use the sd, $\sqrt6 \approx 2.4495$.
byKey.two-tailed: You used 1.96, which leaves 2.5% in the lower tail. The 95% VaR leaves 5%: 1.645.
byKey.triangle: That is the triangle's VaR from part 3. The colleague uses the normal.

explain.text: $N(0, 6)$ has sd $\sqrt6 \approx 2.4495$, and the 5% point is 1.645 sds below the mean. So the VaR is $1.645 \times 2.4495 \approx 4.03$. At 95% the two models nearly agree.

parts.question: Now the 99% VaR, with $P(Z < -2.326) = 0.01$ for the normal and the tail from part 3 for the triangle. By how much, in £k, does the normal 99% VaR exceed the triangle's? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The triangle gives $6 - \sqrt{0.72} \approx 5.15$ and the normal $2.326\sqrt6 \approx 5.70$. The gap is $5.70 - 5.15 = 0.55$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find each 99% VaR, then subtract the triangle's from the normal's.

byKey.sign: You took the normal's VaR from the triangle's. The normal's is the larger one.
byKey.at-95: That is the 95% gap, $4.03 - 4.10$, from parts 3 and 4. Redo both at 99%.
byKey.variance: You multiplied 2.326 by the variance 6. Use the sd, $\sqrt6$.

explain.text: The triangle's tail gives $(6 - v)^2 = 0.72$, so $v = 6 - \sqrt{0.72} \approx 5.15$. The normal gives $2.326 \times 2.4495 \approx 5.70$, which is 0.55 higher. The triangle stops at £6k, so this far out the normal's tail is the fatter one.

items.prose: A share trades at £40 with drift $m = 4\%$ and volatility $\sigma = 35\%$ a year. If the issuer survives the year, $S_1 = 40\,e^{(m - \sigma^2/2) + \sigma Z}$ with $Z \sim N(0, 1)$. The issuer defaults at an exponential time with hazard rate $\lambda = 0.05$ a year, independently of $Z$, and the share is then worth £0.

parts.question: What is the chance the issuer survives the year? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The time to default $T$ has $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$.

byKey.rate: That is $1 - \lambda$. The survival chance is $e^{-\lambda}$, a little higher.
byKey.default: That is the chance of default within the year. Take it from 1.

explain.text: The time to default $T$ is exponential with $\lambda = 0.05$, so $P(T > t) = e^{-0.05t}$. A year's survival is $e^{-0.05} \approx 0.9512$. That is a little above $1 - 0.05$, because the hazard applies only while the issuer is alive.

parts.question: Given the issuer survives, what is $E[S_1]$, in pounds? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A lognormal's mean adds $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$ back to the log drift.

byKey.median: That is the median, $40e^{0.04 - 0.06125}$. The mean adds back the drag.
byKey.today: That is today's price. With drift 4% the mean price grows by $e^{0.04}$.

explain.text: The lognormal mean is $40e^{(m - \sigma^2/2) + \sigma^2/2} = 40e^{m}$. So the expected price given survival is $40e^{0.04} \approx \text{£}41.63$. The drag $\tfrac{0.35^2}{2} \approx 0.0613$ moves the median, not the mean.

parts.question: Using 0.9512 from part 1 and £41.63 from part 2, what is $E[S_1]$ before you know whether the issuer survives? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight each outcome by its chance: default leaves the share at £0.

byKey.survives: That is the mean given survival from part 2. Default, with chance 0.0488, leaves £0.
byKey.linear: You used $0.95$ for the survival chance. Part 1 gave 0.9512.
byKey.median: You weighted the median £39.16. An expected price uses the mean, £41.63.

explain.text: Split on default: the share is worth 0 with chance 0.0488 and averages £41.63 otherwise. So $E[S_1] \approx 0.9512 \times 41.63 \approx 39.60$, below today's £40. A positive drift does not make up for a 5% hazard.

parts.question: Given the issuer survives, what is the chance the share ends the year above £40? Find $z$ to the nearest 0.01, using $\Phi(0.06) = 0.5239$ and $\Phi(0.11) = 0.5438$ as needed. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Standardise $\ln(40/40) = 0$ with the log drift $m - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$.

byKey.phi: That is $\Phi(0.06) = P(S_1 < 40)$. Take it from 1 for the chance of ending above.
byKey.no-drag: You used the drift 0.04 alone, so $z \approx 0.11$. The log drift is $0.04 - 0.06125$.
byKey.half: That treats £40 as the median. The drag pulls the median down to £39.16.

explain.text: $\ln(40/40) = 0$ and the log drift is $0.04 - 0.06125 = -0.02125$. So $z = \tfrac{0.02125}{0.35} \approx 0.06$ and $P(S_1 > 40 \mid \text{survives}) = 1 - \Phi(0.06) = 0.4761$. Even a survivor is more likely down than up.

parts.question: Now drop the condition. Using 0.9512 from part 1 and 0.4761 from part 4, what is $P(S_1 > 40)$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ending above £40 needs survival and a rise.

byKey.survivor: That is the chance given survival, from part 4. A default leaves the share at £0, below £40.
byKey.no-drag: That carries part 4's slip of leaving out the drag. Use 0.4761 from part 4.

explain.text: A default leaves the share at 0, so ending above £40 needs survival and a rise. Independence multiplies the two: $0.9512 \times 0.4761 \approx 0.4529$. Despite a positive drift, the share ends up less than half the time.
